claims.case_section: Section 5: Blending vs. Showfolk Contact Hypotheses
claims.short_label: hocus(-pocus) × bunkum blending hypothesis vs. British mummers' patter, Anglo-Romani hokkano, and 'oakum' folk etymology
claims.statement: American theatrical 'hokum' is most plausibly analyzed as a blend of 'hocus(-pocus)' and 'bunkum' in late-19th-century variety slang—potentially reinforced by British mummers' formulaic 'hokum' patter (1857-1864) or Anglo-Romani 'hokkano'/'hokkeny' ('deception, trick')—whereas 1907-1936 backstage 'oakum'/'hoakum' explanations reflect secondary folk-etymological rationalization.
claims.rationale: Both 'hocus' and 'bunkum' were active in 19th-century American theatrical vocabulary, whereas performers' own 1909 Variety letters ('hocum' vs. 'oakum') show guesswork after the word was already established.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Pre-1899 currency of 'hocus'/'hoky-poky' and 'bunkum' alongside documented British mummers' 'hokum' formulas and Anglo-Romani 'hokkano-' stems.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Conclusive proof choosing 'hocus × bunkum' blending over Anglo-Romani showfolk borrowing or remodeling of stage name 'Hokum'.

limitations: Blending, Romani showfolk contact, and comic-name lexicalization could have converged rather than acting mutually exclusively.
resolution_criteria: Locate an 1889-1899 New York Clipper or Dramatic Mirror passage bridging the comic character name 'Hokum' (1889) or 'hocus/bunkum' phrasing directly into common-noun 'hokum'.
